{:db/id "question-15361c81-aace-5a26-b7c5-2e82d38f451f" :question/id #uuid "15361c81-aace-5a26-b7c5-2e82d38f451f" :question/math-academy-id "q-135349" :question/problem "$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}],\,q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $q$ is the steady-state vector of the stochastic matrix $P$ shown above, what is the value of $a+b-c?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0.1 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & 0.1 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & 0.2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.9 & 0.4 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.6 & -0.9 & 0.3 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=10{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=10{R}_{2} \\ {R}_{3}:=10{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 6 & -9 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 19 & -19 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -19 & 19 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{2}={x}_{3}.
$$

 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{3}-8{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}={x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{3}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{3} & =1 \\ 3{x}_{3} & =1 \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b-c=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0e744f0f-1893-571c-a245-886e0be7796d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "fbc10db1-83ee-5f40-90d1-b581f73d6e92" :question/math-academy-id "q-135412" :question/problem "A study determines how customers' yearly preferences change between the LB and SB telephone companies. The table below describes the results of this study.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **LB** | **SB** |
| To: | **LB** | $0$ | $0.25$ |
| **SB** | $1$ | $0.75$ |  |

It's found that $100%$ of the customers who currently use the LB company will choose the SB company next year, while $25%$ of the customers who currently use the SB company will use the LB company next year.

Assuming that there are $100\,000$ customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, determine the number of customers who will eventually use the SB company." :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, note that

$$
{P}^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.187\,5 \\ 0.75 & 0.812\,5\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 \\ 1 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{4}{5}$ of the customers will eventually use the SB company. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this company is

$$
\frac{4}{5}\cdot 100\,000=80\,000.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f22ac3a1-3b1b-5c02-9aac-e44227bf9c37"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "A study determines how customers' yearly preferences change between the LB and SB telephone companies. The table below describes the results of this study.

|  |  | From: |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | **LB** | **SB** |
| To: | **LB** | $0$ | $0.25$ |
| **SB** | $1$ | $0.75$ |  |

It's found that $100%$ of the customers who currently use the LB company will choose the SB company next year, while $25%$ of the customers who currently use the SB company will use the LB company next year.

Assuming that there are $100\,000$ customers in total and that the given probabilities remain constant over many years, determine the number of customers who will eventually use the SB company."] ["question-fbc10db1-83ee-5f40-90d1-b581f73d6e92" :question/worked-solution "From the table, we get the corresponding stochastic matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, note that

$$
{P}^{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.187\,5 \\ 0.75 & 0.812\,5\end{aligned}].
$$

The matrix ${P}^{2}$ contains only positive entries. So, the matrix $P$ is regular. As a result, after many years, the distribution will eventually converge to the unique steady-state vector of $P,$ and this convergence does not depend on the initial state.

Recall that a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P$ is a stochastic vector $q$ such that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq=q\,⟹\,(P-I)q=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $P-I,$ we get

$$
P-I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.25 \\ 1 & 0.75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 \\ 1 & -0.25\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the matrix equation $(P-I)q=0$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.25 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
q=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, $\frac{4}{5}$ of the customers will eventually use the SB company. Therefore, the number of customers who will eventually use this company is

$$
\frac{4}{5}\cdot 100\,000=80\,000.
$$"] ["question-fbc10db1-83ee-5f40-90d1-b581f73d6e92" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f22ac3a1-3b1b-5c02-9aac-e44227bf9c37" :answer-field/id #uuid 17592186125565 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125849 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a stochastic matrix $P$ and a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}.$ Then, $\mathbf{q}$ is a **steady-state vector** of $P$ if 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

For example, to show that the stochastic vector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

is a steady-state vector for the stochastic matrix 

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]
$$

 

we compute the matrix product $P\mathbf q\mathbin:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0.94+2\cdot 0.03 \\ 0.06+2\cdot 0.97\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =q\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P\mathbf q = \mathbf q,$ the vector $\mathbf q$ is a steady-state vector of $P.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e1601d67-32bc-5796-a800-6e704f25f991" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5500 :tutorial/title "Steady-State Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "965fe16f-9c57-5058-9e32-90332314977c" :step/math-academy-id 34230 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125566}} {:db/id 17592186125566 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124615 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124426 :question/id #uuid "8914449a-3d6f-5847-9e94-3be0a2ccbc94" :question/math-academy-id "e-9178"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f4f2f4f4-af4a-597d-b6c6-afb82e708fc2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049585} {:db/id 17592186050825}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124770} {:db/id 17592186124771} {:db/id 17592186269024} {:db/id 17592186269025} {:db/id 17592186269026} {:db/id 17592186269027}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Steady-State Vectors of Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "bd127c03-d025-5b21-ae93-e24b7aec916f" :step/math-academy-id 34231 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125567}} {:db/id 17592186125567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125850 :tutorial/content "To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that 

$$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute $(P-I):$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "78f635ff-e2e7-5c9f-9ec2-470187a45bc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5501 :tutorial/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "A stochastic matrix $P$ is **regular** if there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $P^n$ has all positive elements.

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

- The stochastic matrix $Q,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

 
contains a zero element. However, if we compute its square, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

 
which has all positive elements. Therefore, $Q$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Regular stochastic matrices have the following important property:

> *Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain
> 
> 
> $$
> \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
> $$
> 
> 
> converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and 

\[
P^n \mathbf{q}_0 \to \mathbf{q} 
\]

as [math]n \to \infty.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "255fadf0-9fc2-52d5-976b-015a97f52b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5502 :tutorial/title "Regular Stochastic Matrices"} :step/id #uuid "735b7b96-43fa-5c0e-b4b8-df7598a6610b" :step/math-academy-id 34235 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125568}} {:db/id 17592186125588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]
$$

 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{aligned}] \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{aligned}]\approx [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{aligned}]\approx [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers." :tutorial/id #uuid "cb9435c4-44ed-58ec-9c04-b8fed4403fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6151 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7c429a3d-9dd8-5fe2-a7e7-cf0e9f515d1a" :step/math-academy-id 37332 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125565}}] :activity/title "Steady-State Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124712} {:db/id 17592186125588 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. $$
P\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}.
$$

Let's begin by writing this equation in a slightly different form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Pq & =q \\ Pq-q & =0 \\ Pq-Iq & =0 \\ (P-I)q & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector we seek is a solution to the matrix equation $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's use this idea to find a steady-state vector for the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute $(P-I):$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, to solve $(P-I)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{0},$ we reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0.75 & -0.5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-0.75 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
x_1= \dfrac 23 x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Since the steady-state vector must be stochastic, its entries should add up to $1.$ Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2} & =1 \\ \frac{5}{3}{x}_{2} & =1 \\ {x}_{2} & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, our steady-state vector is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "78f635ff-e2e7-5c9f-9ec2-470187a45bc3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5501 :tutorial/title "Finding the Steady-State Vector of a Stochastic Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "429ea8df-33bc-5c79-a0d6-97b71166cd98" :step/math-academy-id 34232 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125570}} {:db/id 17592186125850 :tutorial/content "To find a steady-state vector of a stochastic matrix $P,$ we seek a stochastic vector $\mathbf{q}$ such that

Let's consider some examples:

- The stochastic matrix $P,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0.75 & 0.5\end{aligned}]
$$

 
has all positive elements. Therefore, it is a regular stochastic matrix.

$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0.5 \\ 1 & 0.5\end{aligned}]

> *Any regular stochastic matrix has a **unique** steady-state vector $\mathbf q.$ Moreover, the Markov chain
> 
> 
> $$

> $$
> 
> 
> converges to $\mathbf q$ for **any** initial state $\mathbf x_0.$*

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and 

\[
P^n \mathbf{q}_0 \to \mathbf{q} 
\]

In other words, if [math]P[/math] is a regular [math]m \times m[/math] stochastic matrix and [math]\mathbf{q}_0 \in \mathbf{R}^m[/math] is an arbitrary (initial) stochastic vector, then [math]P[/math] has the unique steady state vector [math]\mathbf{q}[/math] and

as [math]n \to \infty.[/math]" :tutorial/id #uuid "255fadf0-9fc2-52d5-976b-015a97f52b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5502 :tutorial/title "Regular Stochastic Matrices"} {:db/id 17592186125855 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

- $6\%$ of the city population relocates to the countryside,

- $3\%$ of the countryside population relocates to the city, and

- everyone else remains where they are.

Additionally, $70\%$ of the population lived in the city and $30\%$ in the countryside at the time of the study. 

We can represent this situation using a stochastic matrix $P$ and initial state vector $\mathbf x_0,$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}0.94 & 0.03 \\ 0.06 & 0.97\end{aligned}]
$$

 

As we've seen, to find the state vector $\mathbf x_{k+1}$ that corresponds to the $(k+1)$th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the $k$th year by $P.$ This gives rise to the following Markov chain:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}, \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}, \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}, \\ ⋮ & \,⋮ \\ {x}_{k+1} & =P{x}_{k} \\ ⋮ & \,⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The local authority wants to determine whether the state vectors settle down to a fixed state. With the aid of a computer, they compute the following states:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =P{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0.667 \\ 0.333\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2} & =P{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0.636\,97 \\ 0.363\,03\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{3} & =P{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0.609\,64 \\ 0.390\,36\end{aligned}] \\  & ⋮ \\ {x}_{100} & =P{x}_{99}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,363 \\ 0.666\,637\end{aligned}]\approx [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{101} & =P{x}_{100}=[\begin{aligned}0.333\,36 \\ 0.666\,64\end{aligned}]\approx [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the data, we see that the vectors $\mathbf x_{100}$ and $\mathbf x_{101}$ are both approximately equal to the vector

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Furthermore, computing $\mathbf x_{102}, \mathbf{x}_{103}, \ldots$ all give vectors approximately equal to $\mathbf q.$ This suggests that the sequence $\mathbf x_k$ converges to $\mathbf q\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_k \rightarrow \mathbf q \quad\textrm{as}\quad k\to\infty.
$$

The vector $\mathbf q$ is called a **steady-state vector** of the matrix $P.$ Here, our steady-state vector suggests that after enough time has passed, one-third of the population will live in the city and two-thirds will live in the countryside.

Finally, notice that for large values of $k,$ we have

$$
P\mathbf x_k \approx \mathbf x_{k}.
$$

This observation indicates how to find $\mathbf q$ without resorting to computers." :tutorial/id #uuid "cb9435c4-44ed-58ec-9c04-b8fed4403fcd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6151 :tutorial/title
